topicName: Migrations, Schema Evolution, and Zero-Downtime Deploys
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Migrations, Schema Evolution, and Zero-Downtime Deploys in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"As Ruby on Rails applications scale, managing database schema changes without causing downtime or failing requests becomes critical. Standard migrations can lock tables and block reads or writes, resulting in application outages. This tutorial covers best practices for safe schema evolution and zero-downtime deployments."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Challenge of Schema Locking"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you run standard ActiveRecord migrations like adding a column with a default value or renaming a table, relational databases often place an exclusive lock on the table. During this time, any incoming web requests trying to read from or write to that table will hang or fail."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"The Multi-Step Deployment Pattern"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"To achieve zero-downtime deployments, you must decouple database changes from code changes. This is achieved through a multi-step process often called the Expand and Contract pattern:"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Phase 1 (Expand): Add the new database column as nullable, keeping the old column intact."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Phase 2 (Migrate Code): Deploy application code that writes to both columns and reads from the old column (or falls back to the new one)."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Phase 3 (Backfill): Run a background job or rake task to copy historical data from the old column to the new column."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Phase 4 (Switch): Deploy code that exclusively reads and writes to the new column."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Phase 5 (Contract): Remove the old column in a subsequent deployment."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Example: Renaming a Column Safely"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Suppose we want to rename a column from 'first_name' to 'given_name' on the 'users' table. Directly running rename_column would cause errors for older application instances still referencing 'first_name'. Instead, follow these steps:"},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"class AddGivenNameToUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change
    add_column :users, :given_name, :string
  end
end"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, configure your ActiveRecord model to populate both columns during writes, ensuring backward compatibility with any running nodes:"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"class User < ApplicationRecord
  before_save :sync_names

  private

  def sync_names
    if attribute_changed?(:first_name)
      self.given_name = first_name
    end
  end
end"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Adding Indexes Without Blocking Writes"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Adding an index on a large table normally blocks writes in PostgreSQL and MySQL. In PostgreSQL, you can use CONCURRENTLY to build the index in the background without locking the table. Rails supports this option natively in modern versions:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"class AddIndexUsersEmailConcurrently < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  disable_ddl_transaction!

  def change
    add_index :users, :email, algorithm: :concurrently
  end
end"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Note that disable_ddl_transaction! is required because concurrent index creation cannot run inside a traditional database transaction."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Zero-downtime deployments require discipline and careful planning. By breaking schema changes into smaller, backward-compatible steps, utilizing gems like strong_migrations to catch dangerous queries, and leveraging concurrent operations, you can evolve your Rails database without disrupting your users."}]
